tytul: How to Actually Do Your Therapy Homework (When the Week Eats It)
tresc_html:
In the room it sounded easy. Notice the thought, write down what came before it, bring it back next week. By Wednesday night the only part still alive is a low hum of having let someone down. Then Tuesday arrives and you hear yourself say the week got away from you.

How common this is, and what the numbers really say

Skipping the homework is closer to the norm than to the exception. Tang and Kreindler, writing in JMIR Mental Health in 2017, report that surveys of practitioners put non-adherence among adult clients at roughly 20% to 50%, and around 50% in adolescents.

Those numbers come from clinicians estimating their own caseloads, not from researchers counting returned worksheets, so treat them as a rough scale rather than a measurement. The same paper mentions something else worth sitting with: in automated programs with little therapist involvement, non-completion has run as high as 40%. Nobody has solved this with a reminder.

The one thing the numbers do settle: if you have been carrying your undone homework around as a private character flaw, it is a very crowded secret.

Why the task dies between Tuesday and Sunday

It was never specific enough to start

"Notice when you get anxious this week" is not a task. It is a subject heading. A task has a trigger, an action and a stopping point, and you can tell afterwards whether it happened. "Pay attention to your thoughts" fails all three tests, which is why it quietly becomes nothing.

It cost more than it looked like it would cost

You agree to things in the room with your therapist's full attention on you, 40 minutes of momentum behind you, and a version of yourself who has just spent an hour thinking carefully about their own life. That person is not the one who gets the task. The one who gets it is you at 9pm on a Wednesday, having eaten standing up.

Avoidance is the point

Plenty of between-session work aims straight at the thing you most want to leave alone. Write the message you have been putting off. Sit with the feeling instead of reaching for your phone. Go to the thing. When that task does not happen, the problem is not really your calendar. The task is working as designed, and the design includes resistance.

Nobody was going to read it

School homework got collected. Therapy homework often does not. If the last four tasks were never mentioned again, you have learned something accurate about the incentives, and part of the fix belongs to the next session rather than to your week. Kazantzis and colleagues, in their 2021 model of homework in Cognitive Therapy and Research, treat reviewing the task as a step in its own right rather than an optional courtesy.

What the research says helps

Three things here have decent evidence behind them, and every one of them comes with a catch.

Start with whether the work matters at all. Kazantzis, Whittington and Dattilio pooled 46 studies covering 1,072 people in a 2010 meta-analysis in Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice. Comparing controlled studies that ran the same therapy with and without homework, the homework conditions came out ahead at d = 0.48. Moderate, and every bit of it earned on days nobody was watching.

Then how much of it you do. A 2016 meta-analysis by Kazantzis and colleagues in Behavior Therapy covered 17 studies and 2,312 clients. Narrowed to how much people completed against their symptoms at the end of treatment, it came out at g = 0.79, across 15 of those studies and 1,537 clients. The catch: this one is correlational. People who are already improving may find the tasks easier to face, so the arrow could point either way.

Last, the part you can act on tonight. Deciding when and where beats deciding to try harder. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 meta-analysis in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology gathered 94 independent studies and more than 8,000 participants on if-then plans, and found d = 0.65 on goal attainment. That evidence mostly comes from ordinary goals, exercise and health screening and the like, not from therapy tasks. Borrow the mechanism, do not import the number.

Make the task smaller than your worst day

The if-then version of the task

Before you leave, turn the agreement into one sentence with a time and a place in it. The shape is: when this specific thing happens, I will do this specific small action, here. So "track your anxiety this week" becomes "when I get back to my desk after a meeting, I write one line in my phone about what my body did." One of those you can complete. The other you can only feel guilty about.

The two minute floor

Then write the version you could still do on your worst day this month. Flu, deadline, three hours of sleep. If the task is a thought record, the floor is one line. If it is a walk, the floor is the end of the street. The floor is not the goal and it is not cheating. It is what stops a bad week turning into a lapsed month, and one line is still something to read back later, which beats an ambitious plan that stopped in week two.

One place where it lives

Decide where the task is written down before you need it. Not four places. One. A task spread across your memory, a text you sent yourself, a photo of your therapist's notebook and a half-remembered intention is a task with no address.

[FEATURE: homework | What you agreed to try lands on your home screen as a to do for today, instead of surfacing guiltily at the next session.]

What to do when you did not do it

Bring the failure as data, not as a confession

"I did not do it, sorry" ends the conversation. "I did not do it, and here is where it stopped" starts one. Where it stopped is useful information about you, and your therapist would rather have that than a clean report.

The three questions worth answering before the next session

Spend two minutes on these, in writing or out loud, at any point before you go in.

  • Where did it stop? You never started, you started and stopped, or you forgot it existed. Those are different problems, and they do not have the same fix.
  • What was happening in the 10 minutes before it should have happened? There is usually a pattern there, and it is usually not laziness.
  • What would have made it 20% easier? A different time of day, a smaller version, doing it with someone, doing it out loud instead of on paper.

If writing that down feels like homework about homework, say it into your phone on the way home. There is a longer case for that in writing it down or saying it out loud.

When to renegotiate the task with your therapist

Twice in a row is the signal. Not "I am failing therapy", but "this task and my life do not fit, and one of them is easier to adjust." Say that out loud. A task nobody can perform is not a test you keep failing, it is a draft that needs another pass. And if what you actually want to know is whether a particular exercise does anything for you specifically, there is a method for that in testing which coping skills actually work.

A week that fits a real week

Four short moments. Twenty minutes across seven days, give or take, and none of it needs a desk.

  1. Before you leave the session, write the task down in your therapist's own words, then write your if-then version underneath it. That takes about 90 seconds, in the car or on the platform.
  2. Set one reminder, for the time and place named in the if-then, and nothing else. A notification at a random Tuesday lunchtime is noise.
  3. After the attempt, write down what it took out of you, not just whether it happened. "Started three times before it stuck, and it was easier than I expected" and "avoided it all week, and the list got heavier every time I looked" are both worth having.
  4. The night before the next session, read those lines back. That is your honest report, and reading it takes less time than reconstructing it.

This slots into the wider rhythm described in a weekly rhythm between sessions, and the report you end up with feeds straight into bringing the honest report to the next session.

[FEATURE: smart-reminders | A nudge at the moment that fits your week, with a separate switch for every type, so you can keep one and turn the rest off.]

MindSync exists because its founder spent 10 years and $130,000 on therapy and watched the agreements made in the room dissolve in the week that followed. It holds the task, the attempt and what it cost in one place, so what you bring back is a record rather than an apology. You can see what the app does. None of it replaces the work, and no reminder has ever done a task for anybody.

[FEATURES: Turning an agreement into something that happens || workspace | The task, the topics and the threads in one place between sessions. || check-ins | A one minute rating that shows what the task actually cost you. || session-prep | The honest report ready before you walk in.]

Frequently asked questions

What is therapy homework?

Therapy homework is whatever you and your therapist agree you will do between appointments: a thought record, a breathing practice, a conversation you have been avoiding, a walk at a set time. It is most associated with cognitive behavioral therapy, but between-session tasks appear under other names across most approaches. The point is to practice where the problem actually lives.

Why can't I do my therapy homework?

Usually for one of four reasons, and laziness is not among them. The task was too vague to start. It cost more than it looked like it would. It pointed straight at what you avoid, so avoiding it was predictable. Or nobody was going to review it, so it quietly stopped mattering. Each of those has a different fix.

What happens if I don't do my therapy homework?

Nothing punitive, and it is worth telling your therapist rather than skating past it. Not doing the task is information about the task, about the week, or about what the task is touching, and all three are useful in the room. Research links completing between-session work with better outcomes, so the move is to adjust the task rather than drop it.

How much therapy homework is normal?

There is no standard dose, and it varies enormously by approach and by therapist. What matters more than the amount is whether the task is specific, whether it fits the week you actually have, and whether it gets reviewed at the next session. If you are being handed more than you can do, that is a conversation to have out loud rather than a standard to quietly fail.

Should I tell my therapist I did not do the homework?

Yes, and preferably in the first five minutes rather than at the end. Where the task broke down is often the most useful thing you bring in that week. Therapists expect this: surveys of practitioners put non-adherence among adult clients somewhere between 20% and 50%, so you are describing a normal week rather than confessing a failure.
